Section 1 of 17

Can You Follow Jesus and Still Be Native?

For some Native people, this question carries generations of pain.

Children were taken from their families. Hair was cut. Native names were replaced. Languages were punished. Cultural practices were condemned without being understood.

Some of this was done by people carrying Bibles and claiming to represent God.

That history can make an invitation to follow Jesus sound like an invitation to stop being Native.

But cultural erasure was never the gospel.

Jesus does not ask you to become white, reject your people, or imitate another culture. He asks you to know the Creator, receive salvation, and place your entire life under His truth.

Following Jesus will change every person. It does not erase the identity the Creator gave them.

The Creator Sees Every People

Read Acts 17:24–28 ↗.

The Creator made every nation and gives life to every person.

No race owns God.

No language has greater access to Him.

No nation is naturally closer to Him.

Read Revelation 7:9–10 ↗.

John saw people from every nation, tribe, people, and language standing before the Creator.

Their differences were still visible. They were united in worship, but they had not become one human culture.

The Creator’s family is diverse and united at the same time.

Culture Is More Than Spiritual Belief

Culture can include:

  • Language
  • Family relationships
  • Names
  • Food
  • Clothing
  • Art
  • Music
  • Humor
  • History
  • Community responsibilities
  • Ways of showing respect
  • Knowledge connected with a place
  • Stories passed through generations
  • Customs surrounding important life events

These parts of identity are not automatically acts of worship.

Speaking a Native language is not worshiping another god.

Wearing culturally meaningful clothing is not automatically a spiritual act.

Creating art, singing, dancing, telling family stories, or gathering as a community is not automatically wrong.

Meaning matters.

A person should understand what a practice actually represents before accepting or rejecting it.

The Bible Does Not Belong to European Culture

Most of the Bible’s human writers came from the ancient Middle East. They lived within Hebrew, Aramaic, Greek, and Roman settings.

Jesus was born into a Jewish family under Roman occupation. His first followers were not European or American.

The Bible was written through people living in real cultures, but its authority stands above every culture.

It examines Native cultures.

It examines European cultures.

It examines modern American culture.

It examines church culture.

It examines online culture.

No culture becomes the Creator’s standard for everyone else.

Scripture is the standard.

Did Jesus Ask People to Give Up Their Ethnic Identity?

Read Acts 15:1–29 ↗.

The first followers of Jesus faced a major conflict. Some people argued that non-Jewish believers needed to adopt Jewish cultural practices before they could fully belong.

The leaders studied the question and concluded that people from other nations did not need to become culturally Jewish to follow Jesus.

They were called to turn away from idolatry and sexual sin, but they were not required to surrender their ethnic identity.

This distinction still matters.

Jesus calls every person away from sin. He does not call everyone into the same human culture.

What Happened at Pentecost?

Read Acts 2:1–11 ↗.

People from many regions and language groups gathered in Jerusalem.

When the Holy Spirit came, He did not force everyone to understand one dominant human language. He enabled people to hear the message in their own languages.

The Creator could have chosen only one language. Instead, He crossed language boundaries to reach people where they were.

Language can carry memory, identity, humor, relationship, and ways of understanding the world.

A Native language does not need to disappear for someone to know Jesus.

Scripture, prayer, music, and teaching can be expressed in the language people understand most deeply.

Does the Creator Accept Everything in Every Culture?

No culture is perfect because every culture is formed by human beings affected by sin.

Every culture contains things that may reflect:

  • Love
  • Courage
  • Generosity
  • Creativity
  • Family loyalty
  • Care for others
  • Respect
  • Justice
  • Responsibility
  • Care for creation

Every culture may also contain beliefs or practices connected with:

  • Pride
  • Violence
  • Sexual wrongdoing
  • Greed
  • Revenge
  • Oppression
  • Dishonesty
  • False worship
  • Spiritual deception
  • Harmful control

The Creator does not condemn one culture while ignoring sin in another.

Read Romans 3:22–23 ↗.

Everyone has sinned. Everyone needs grace. Everyone must allow Scripture to examine their beliefs and actions.

What Is Cultural Erasure?

Cultural erasure happens when people are pressured or forced to abandon their identity so they can be accepted by a more powerful group.

It may include:

  • Punishing a language
  • Replacing a person’s name without permission
  • Treating one style of clothing as morally superior
  • Demanding the loss of family or community ties
  • Teaching people to feel ashamed of their ancestry
  • Treating dominant cultural habits as biblical commands
  • Condemning unfamiliar customs without understanding them
  • Making people imitate another race to appear spiritual

The Creator calls people to repentance from sin. Repentance and cultural erasure are not the same thing.

Repentance turns us away from beliefs and actions that oppose God.

Cultural erasure removes parts of identity because another group considers its own culture superior.

Jesus commands repentance. He does not command racial or cultural superiority.

How Should We Understand the Word “Pagan”?

People sometimes use “pagan” as a quick label for anything unfamiliar.

That approach is careless.

A practice should not be condemned merely because it did not come from Europe or because an outsider does not understand it.

At the same time, a practice should not be accepted merely because it is traditional, old, or culturally meaningful.

The right questions are:

  • What does this practice mean?
  • What spiritual belief stands behind it?
  • Who or what receives honor?
  • Does it involve worship?
  • Does it seek help from another spirit?
  • Does it agree with Scripture?
  • Can I participate while remaining completely loyal to the Creator?

The Bible asks us to understand and test rather than stereotype.

What Is Spiritual Loyalty?

Read Exodus 20:2–6 ↗.

The Creator asks us to worship Him alone.

Knowing God involves more than adding Jesus to a collection of spiritual powers. He asks for complete loyalty.

The God called “Creator” in these guides is the God revealed in the Bible: the Father, Jesus, and the Holy Spirit.

He is not one local spirit among many.

He made the land, sky, water, animals, humanity, and the entire universe. Nothing in creation is equal to Him.

Read Isaiah 45:5–6 ↗.

Giving the Creator complete loyalty does not make you less Native. It means recognizing who alone gives life and deserves worship.

Respecting Creation and Worshiping Creation Are Different

Read Genesis 1:26–31 ↗ and Genesis 2:15 ↗.

The Creator gave human beings responsibility to care for the Earth.

Polluting water, wasting resources, destroying living things through greed, and treating land as if it has no value oppose responsible care.

Read Psalm 24:1 ↗.

The Earth belongs to the Creator.

Respecting land, water, plants, and animals can agree with biblical stewardship. Worshiping a created being or seeking spiritual power from creation does not.

Read Romans 1:20–25 ↗.

Creation points toward the Creator. It should not replace Him.

You can value the land deeply while directing worship to the One who made it.

Honoring Ancestors and Contacting the Dead Are Different

Your family’s history matters.

You can remember people who came before you, speak their names, preserve their stories, care for burial places, and continue what was good in their example.

The Bible itself preserves stories from earlier generations.

Read Hebrews 11:1–40 ↗.

However, the dead are unconscious until the resurrection. They cannot hear prayers, guide the living, or provide protection.

Read Ecclesiastes 9:5–6 ↗.

Remembering a relative is an act of memory.

Seeking that person’s spiritual presence is an attempt to contact the dead.

The first can honor a life. The second conflicts with Scripture and can expose someone to spiritual deception.

How Should Ceremonies Be Evaluated?

The word “ceremony” covers many different activities.

One ceremony may be a social gathering. Another may preserve history. Another may mark a family event. Another may involve prayer, offerings, spirits, or worship.

The name alone does not tell you enough.

Ask:

  • What is the purpose of the ceremony?
  • What words will be spoken?
  • Is prayer involved?
  • To whom is prayer directed?
  • Are spirits invited?
  • Is protection or healing requested from another power?
  • Are the dead addressed as if they are present?
  • Are objects treated as sources of spiritual power?
  • What would my participation communicate?
  • Can I remain loyal to Jesus while taking part?

Do not guess. Ask respectful questions and listen carefully.

If the ceremony includes worship or spiritual involvement that conflicts with Scripture, loyalty to the Creator may require you to decline that part.

Can You Attend Without Participating in Everything?

Sometimes you may attend a gathering because you love your family or want to support your community, while choosing not to participate in a particular spiritual act.

Read 1 Corinthians 10:23–33 ↗.

Paul taught people to consider both personal conscience and what their participation communicates to others.

Your decision may depend on what the event means and what you are expected to do.

You might be able to attend respectfully while remaining silent during a spiritual portion. In another situation, your presence may clearly communicate agreement with worship you cannot support.

Ask the Creator for wisdom.

Read James 1:5 ↗.

You can explain your boundary gently:

“I love you, and I am not rejecting our family. I have chosen to direct my prayer and worship to the Creator through Jesus, so I cannot participate in this part.”

A calm explanation often communicates more love than an angry condemnation.

What If Your Family Feels Rejected?

A change in spiritual belief can affect relationships.

Family members may fear that you now consider yourself superior. They may remember how religion was used to shame Native people. They may worry that you are rejecting your community.

Listen before defending yourself.

Acknowledge the history honestly.

Do not describe your entire culture as evil.

Explain what you believe without insulting what another person values.

Continue showing love through your actions:

  • Stay connected when it is safe.
  • Help with practical needs.
  • Keep your promises.
  • Listen to family stories.
  • Speak respectfully.
  • Protect appropriate cultural knowledge.
  • Serve your community.
  • Admit when you are wrong.
  • Refuse spiritual practices that violate your conscience without rejecting the people involved.

Your life can show that following Jesus has made you more loving and dependable rather than distant and proud.

What If a Church Tells You to Abandon Your Culture?

Ask whether the demand comes from Scripture or human preference.

Does the Bible require you to change your Native name?

Does it forbid your language?

Does it command one culture’s clothing style?

Does it say that one race’s music is naturally holier?

Does it require you to cut healthy ties with your family?

If Scripture does not teach the requirement, no human institution has the right to place that burden on you.

Read Colossians 2:20–23 ↗.

Human rules can appear spiritual while lacking authority from the Creator.

Read Mark 7:7–9 ↗.

Jesus warned against teaching human commands as if they came from God.

Respectful spiritual community should help you follow Scripture. It should not demand cultural imitation.

Can Cultural Forms Be Used to Share Biblical Truth?

Read 1 Corinthians 9:19–23 ↗.

Paul adjusted how he communicated so that different groups could understand the message. He did not change the truth, but he changed his approach.

Biblical teaching can be communicated through:

  • Native languages
  • Contemporary Native art
  • Music
  • Personal testimony
  • Family conversation
  • Community discussion
  • Storytelling
  • Online media
  • Visual symbols whose meaning agrees with Scripture

The form can connect with a culture while the message remains faithful to the Bible.

However, sacred cultural knowledge should never be taken, copied, exposed, or used for marketing without permission.

A person from outside a nation should not invent Native stories or treat distinct nations as one culture.

Native voices should help decide how biblical truth is communicated within their own communities.

What Is Syncretism?

Syncretism means combining spiritual beliefs that do not agree with one another.

For example, someone may speak about Jesus while also seeking guidance from the dead. Another person may read Scripture while believing an object carries spiritual power. Someone may pray to the Creator and then use divination to discover the future.

This mixture may feel inclusive, but it creates divided spiritual loyalty.

Read 1 Kings 18:20–21 ↗.

Elijah asked the people how long they would continue moving between opposing choices.

Read Matthew 6:24 ↗.

Jesus taught that no one can serve two masters.

The Creator welcomes people from every culture, but He does not share worship with other gods or spirits.

Following Jesus means allowing Him to become the final authority.

Did People in the Bible Keep Their Cultural Identity?

Yes.

The Bible mentions people by their nations, families, languages, and places of origin.

Ruth remained known as a Moabite.

Simon was identified as a man from Cyrene.

The woman who spoke with Jesus remained a Samaritan.

The Ethiopian official remained Ethiopian.

The believers at Pentecost heard the message in their own languages.

Read Acts 8:26–39 ↗.

The Ethiopian official accepted the message about Jesus. Scripture does not say that he became culturally Jewish. He returned home with new faith while remaining who he was.

The Creator changed his spiritual direction without erasing his national identity.

What Can We Learn From Daniel?

Read Daniel 1:1–8 ↗.

Daniel was taken from his homeland into Babylon. He was taught a new language, given a Babylonian education, and assigned a new name.

Daniel learned how Babylon worked, but he did not allow Babylon to decide his highest loyalty.

He remained respectful while setting clear boundaries.

Daniel did not reject every part of his education. He rejected what required disobedience to the Creator.

This gives us a useful pattern:

Understand the culture around you.

Recognize what is good.

Identify where loyalty is being tested.

Set respectful boundaries.

Remain faithful to God.

How Can You Make a Wise Decision?

When you are unsure about a cultural or spiritual practice, use this process.

Understand

Ask someone who truly knows the practice to explain its meaning. Avoid rumors and stereotypes.

Pray

Ask the Creator for wisdom and an honest heart.

Study

Look for clear biblical principles rather than one verse taken out of context.

Identify the spiritual direction

Ask whether the practice points toward the Creator or another source of spiritual power.

Consider your participation

Determine what your actions would communicate to family and community.

Seek wise counsel

Speak with trustworthy Native followers of Jesus and others who respect both Scripture and cultural identity.

Respect your conscience

Read Romans 14:22–23 ↗.

Do not participate while believing the action would be unfaithful to God.

Respond with love

If you must decline, explain your choice without condemning the people involved.

Cultural Pride and Cultural Shame

The Creator does not ask you to be ashamed of being Native.

He also warns every person against pride that treats another group as less valuable.

Read Jeremiah 9:23–24 ↗.

Our deepest confidence should come from knowing the Creator.

Healthy cultural identity can say:

“I value my people, language, family, and history.”

Sinful pride says:

“My people are more valuable than other people.”

Cultural shame says:

“My people and identity have no value.”

The Bible corrects both pride and shame.

Every person has equal dignity before the Creator. Every culture needs His truth and grace.

What Does Redemption Look Like?

Redemption means the Creator takes what sin has damaged and brings it under the healing rule of Jesus.

The Creator can redeem:

  • Identity from shame
  • Family relationships from silence
  • Leadership from control
  • Strength from violence
  • Tradition from misunderstanding
  • Community from division
  • Creativity from destructive use
  • Cultural pride from superiority
  • Spiritual longing from deception

Redemption does not mean pretending every belief is true.

It means allowing Jesus to heal, correct, preserve, and transform.

Read Revelation 21:5 ↗.

The Creator says, “Behold, I make all things new.”

He makes things new without making every person identical.

Questions to Ask About Any Tradition

Use these questions whenever you need clarity:

  1. What is the history and actual meaning of this tradition?
  2. Is it social, cultural, spiritual, or a mixture?
  3. Does it involve prayer or worship?
  4. Who or what receives spiritual honor?
  5. Does it seek contact with the dead or another spirit?
  6. Does it treat an object as a source of supernatural power?
  7. Does it agree with clear biblical teaching?
  8. What kind of character does it produce?
  9. Can I participate with complete loyalty to Jesus?
  10. What will my participation communicate to others?
  11. Can I maintain family love while setting a spiritual boundary?
  12. Have I listened before reaching a conclusion?

Think About It

Write your answers in your own words.

  1. What parts of your cultural identity are most meaningful to you?
  2. Have you ever felt that knowing Jesus required you to become less Native?
  3. What is the difference between repentance and cultural erasure?
  4. What does Pentecost teach about language and the Creator’s message?
  5. How can you distinguish respect for creation from worship of creation?
  6. How can you honor ancestors without seeking contact with the dead?
  7. Is there a cultural or religious practice you would like to understand more clearly?
  8. What questions should you ask before participating in a ceremony?
  9. How could you explain a spiritual boundary without rejecting your family?
  10. Have you accepted a church tradition that may not come from Scripture?
  11. What cultural gift could you use to communicate biblical truth?
  12. What would it mean for Jesus to redeem rather than erase your identity?

Try This During the Coming Week

Set aside fifteen quiet minutes each day.

Read one passage:

  • Day 1: Acts 17:22–31 ↗
  • Day 2: Acts 2:1–12 ↗
  • Day 3: Acts 15:1–29 ↗
  • Day 4: Daniel 1:1–21 ↗
  • Day 5: 1 Corinthians 10:23–33 ↗
  • Day 6: Revelation 7:9–17 ↗
  • Day 7: Revelation 21:22–27 ↗

After each reading, write down:

  • What does this passage teach about culture or identity?
  • What truth applies to every person?
  • What human tradition is being questioned?
  • What does loyalty to the Creator require?
  • How can truth be practiced with respect?

Choose one part of your cultural identity for which you are grateful. Thank the Creator for it.

Then choose one belief or practice you need to examine more carefully through Scripture. Begin with listening, prayer, and honest study.

A Prayer You Can Pray

Creator God, thank You for giving every person dignity and for gathering people from every nation, tribe, and language. Heal the shame and pain caused when Your name was used to erase Native identity. Help me value my family, people, language, and history without placing any culture above Your truth. Give me wisdom to understand traditions before judging them. Show me what is good, what needs healing, and what conflicts with Your Word. Help me direct all prayer, worship, and spiritual loyalty to You through Jesus. Give me courage to set boundaries with humility and love. Redeem my identity and use my life to bring truth, healing, and hope to my community. Amen.

Remember This

Following Jesus does not require becoming less Native.

The Creator’s family includes every nation, tribe, people, and language.

Culture includes much more than spiritual belief.

A cultural practice should be understood before it is evaluated.

No culture is perfect, and no culture is the standard for every other culture.

Scripture stands above Native, European, American, and church traditions.

Respecting creation is different from worshiping creation.

Remembering ancestors is different from seeking guidance from the dead.

Repentance turns us away from sin. Cultural erasure removes identity to satisfy a dominant group.

The Creator asks for complete spiritual loyalty without demanding cultural imitation.

Native voices should help shape how biblical truth is shared in Native communities.

Jesus redeems identity rather than erasing it.
